title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Georgia: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Georgia: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Georgia: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: Coordinating healthcare, social benefits, and legal authority for a family member living with an incurable or terminal illness in Georgia draws directly on the Law on Patient Rights, the Law on Health Care, and the Civil Code [1] [2] [3]. We outline five practical steps so families can use Georgia's explicit written advance-will provisions, palliative care rules, and notarial tools before decision-making capacity declines [1] [2] [4].

steps.title: Establish palliative and hospice care coverage
steps.html:
• Access palliative and hospice pathways: Under the Law of Georgia on Health Care, palliative and hospice care for incurably ill patients with limited life expectancy are recognized forms of medical care delivered by specialized multidisciplinary palliative teams [2].
  • Verify state healthcare program eligibility: Contact the Ministry of Health 24/7 hotline (1505) or the Public Service Hall (House of Justice) information line to check Universal Health Care and municipal palliative care or home-care program enrollment; dial 112 for urgent ambulance dispatch [2] [7].
  • Preserve confidentiality and patient access: Under Articles 19 to 21 and Article 27 of the Law on Patient Rights, a competent adult patient may designate a specific person authorized to receive diagnostic and medical status information and instruct clinicians on plain-language explanations [1].

steps.title: Record an advance written directive and medical proxy
steps.html:
• Put an advance medical declaration in writing: Under the Law on Patient Rights, an adult patient who retains decision-making capacity may express an advance will in writing (consent or refusal) covering resuscitation, life-supporting measures, palliative treatment, or hospice care in the event they later lose consciousness or decision-making ability [1].
  • Store copies with family and treating hospital: Place the signed written directive in the inpatient or outpatient medical chart and provide copies to the designated family representative so attending teams have clear authorization [1].
  • Know refusal and consent safeguards: Under the Law on Health Care and Law on Patient Rights, medical interventions require informed consent unless life-saving emergency intervention is immediately required when no representative is reachable [1] [2].

steps.title: Grant a notarized power of attorney for finances and state filings
steps.html:
• Avoid delays if capacity is lost: Under the Civil Code of Georgia and the Law of Georgia on Notaries, a general or specific Power of Attorney allows a chosen family member or agent to deal with banks, Social Service Agency filings, and Public Service Hall offices [3] [4].
  • Certify through a Georgian notary: Visit any licensed notary via the Notary Chamber of Georgia (or request a home or hospital notarial visit for bedbound patients, or video-notarial options where eligible) so banking and property transactions remain valid if illness progresses [4] [8].
  • Review court guardianship triggers: If a person loses capacity without an advance power of attorney, courts must appoint a supporter under Civil Code psychosocial capacity provisions, which takes significantly longer than proactive notarial authorization [3].

steps.title: Check disability status and social assistance allowances
steps.html:
• Register medical-social disability status: Ask the treating specialist to prepare the clinical summary needed for medical-social disability classification so the patient can access state social packages or needs-based aid under the Law on Social Assistance [2] [5].
  • Confirm single-window applications: Submit disability or targeted social assistance applications and check pension delivery routing through Public Service Hall desks or Public Service Development Agency (PSDA) records if identity documents need renewal [5] [6] [7].
  • Verify bank access and standing instructions: Check that bank cards, pension accounts, and authorized signatories are up to date while the patient can confirm instructions directly [3] [4].

steps.title: Organize a will, asset list, and tax overview
steps.html:
• Draft or update a Georgian will: Under Book Six of the Civil Code and the Law on Notaries, a capable adult can execute a written will (typically certified by a notary so it is entered into the electronic inheritance registry) specifying shares for heirs [3] [4] [8].
  • Check tax exemptions for close relatives: Under Article 82 of the Tax Code of Georgia, gifts or inherited assets transferred between first and second line family members are exempt from personal income tax (and up to GEL 150,000 per tax year for third and fourth line heirs) [9].
  • Prepare cross-border authentication if assets span borders: If documents issued in Georgia must be presented abroad later, verify apostille requirements with the Public Service Development Agency [6] [10].

closingQuestion: Are you focusing first on putting a written advance healthcare directive in place or arranging a notarized power of attorney in Georgia?

contacts.name: Notary Chamber of Georgia
contacts.note: Official hotline (+995 32 220 67 77) and notary directory for powers of attorney, wills, and hospital-bedside or remote notarial requests.

contacts.name: Public Service Hall (House of Justice)
contacts.note: Unified service centers across Georgia accepting social assistance applications, property records, and ID renewals.

contacts.name: Public Service Development Agency (PSDA)
contacts.note: Issues civil status certificates, ID cards, and Hague Apostilles for documents used internationally.
